title: Corporate Accountability and Sustainable Food Systems Transitions

Strategies for strengthening corporate accountability in the context of sustainable food system transitions will also be explored. The webinar is intended to be structured as a debate with each panellist providing their perspectives on this topic as well as opportunity for panellists to respond to each other and answer audience questions.

description: This webinar examines how profit-driven financial investors impact poorly regulated healthcare systems in LMICs like India, analyzing patterns of oligopolistic corporatisation and effects on hospital management and frontline providers. Jointly organized by UNU-IIGH and the People's Health Movement, the session presents two recent papers on healthcare financialisation in India with global dimensions.

title: Financialization and the Economics of Health for All
description: This side event catalyzes discussion on how WHO and member states can operationalize the recommendations of WHO's Council on the Economics of Health for All and ensure that WHO's draft strategy (2026-2030) contributes to transformative economic change. It challenges the promotion of private commercial investment for Universal Health Coverage, arguing that profit-driven financing deepens health inequalities, erodes public health values, and weakens democratic oversight. The session calls for a cross-sectoral approach that places health for all at the center of development policy and finance, grounded in equity and sustainability.
partners: Geneva Global Health Hub (G2H2), Public Services International (PSI), Society for International Development (SID)

title: Chasing Accountability in Global Health
description: This Collective Conversation examines the context for the creation of the Independent Accountability Panel (IAP) in 2016 and its dissolution in 2020 as a case study of high hopes, missed opportunities, and planned project failure. It shares four lessons for why meaningful accountability has been so elusive in global health and how future efforts might benefit: the need for normative grounding, institutional legitimacy, genuine independence, and conceptual clarity on accountability. The discussion argues that the deeply neoliberal and colonial architecture of global health governance constrains possibilities for transformative accountability.
partners: The Collective for the Political Determinants of Health, University of Oslo

title: UNU – ATNi Expert Meeting on Corporate Accountability

accountability in the food and beverage sector, complementing existing initiatives such as ATNi’s Indexes. 
The event addresses key gaps (such as how to incorporate qualitative and anecdotal evidence on 
corporate influence) and explore how different actors and tools can work together. It aims to serve as an entry point toward a shared plan of action to strengthen effective corporate accountability.

keyOutputs:
Participants will build a shared understanding of key challenges and approaches, drawing on diverse expert perspectives, and identify relevant data and methodologies to address existing gaps. They will highlight opportunities for collaboration, including which actors are best placed to lead specific elements of the corporate accountability system, and develop a clear outline of how corporate monitoring can drive 
meaningful, real-world impact.

title: Conversation with Sara Hossain on Rights, Justice, and Action
description: This open dialogue brought together legal, feminist, and political economy perspectives from the Global South to examine how gender justice was challenged and defended amid shrinking civic space and rising authoritarianism. The discussion explored how backlash operated through laws, courts, administrative practices, and social norms that legitimized exclusion and silenced critical voices. Grounded in Global South experiences, the conversation reflected on where progress had stalled or reversed. It also highlighted creative legal, institutional, and community-based strategies that continued to sustain and advance women’s rights and gender equality in difficult political environments.
keyOutputs:
Generated a shared understanding of how gender backlash operated through legal reforms, administrative practices, political narratives and social norms.

Highlighted Global South feminist perspectives on the links between gender justice, authoritarianism, shrinking civic space, political economy, and health.

Identified examples of legal, institutional, and community-based strategies used to defend women’s rights and gender equality in difficult political environments.

Strengthened UNU-IIGH engagement on gender justice, rights-based approaches, intersectionality, and the political determinants of health.

title: Gender-responsive/-transformative interventions in HIV, TB, and Malaria programmes: What can we learn from the existing evidence-base?
description: The webinar explored how gender-responsive and gender-transformative interventions can strengthen HIV, TB and malaria programmes and improve both health and gender-related outcomes. It presented findings from a rapid review conducted by UNU-IIGH in partnership with the Global Fund, synthesizing evidence on what works to advance health equity, gender equality and human rights in infectious disease responses.
keyOutputs:
-Launched the rapid evidence review on gender-responsive and gender-transformative interventions in HIV, TB and malaria.
-Shared key findings, promising practices and lessons for stronger gender-focused programming.
-Highlighted policy, donor, research and community perspectives on applying the evidence.
-Created space for exchange of questions, reflections and recommendations.
Shared the full report, summary and recording as follow-up resources.

It focused on strengthening regional solidarity, reviewing advocacy priorities, and identifying pathways for the recognition, regularisation and protection of CHWs as part of the health workforce. Discussions also linked CHW organising to decent work, care economy and climate-sensitive labour protection agendas.
partners: PSI and UNu IIGH
keyOutputs:
-Strengthened regional solidarity and coordination among CHW leaders and unions.
-Shared country-level organising experiences, achievements and challenges.
-Reviewed advocacy priorities on recognition, regularisation, wages, benefits and union rights.
-Updated the Charter of Demands across key domains, including occupational safety and dignity at work.

title: Convening Feminist Mobilization for Advancing Women’s Health, SRHR & GBV

It focused on advancing women’s health, SRHR, bodily autonomy, and GBV prevention amid anti-rights pushback, shrinking civic space, funding cuts, and climate-related challenges. Participants exchanged experiences and shaped regional priorities for Women Deliver 2026 and the Feminist Playbook.
partners: UNFPA with ARROW, Equality Fund, Fos Feminista, UNU IIGH

-Strengthened cross-regional feminist dialogue and alliance-building across Asia, the Pacific, and the Caribbean.
-Identified shared priorities for protecting SRHR, bodily autonomy, and GBV prevention.
-Discussed strategies to counter anti-rights pushback, pronatalist narratives, and shrinking civic space.
-Generated inputs toward an Asia-Pacific Feminist Accountability and Mobilization Framework and Women Deliver 2026 Feminist Playbook

title: Webinar: For Every Generation: Faith, Justice and Science in Immunization.
description: The 90-minute webinar, on Thursday 30 April at 15:00 CET- “For Every Generation: Faith, Justice and Science in Immunizations,” held during World Immunisation Week, brings together World Health Organization (WHO), experts, faith leaders, and scientific experts working at the interface of faith and science to explore how vaccines protect people across the life course. It will review the history and scientific evidence for immunisation, highlighting how vaccines safeguard children, adolescents, adults, and older persons, and why equitable access is a matter of health justice. The webinar will celebrate the contributions of faith-based organisations and the WCC in promoting immunisation and delivering services in communities, while also confronting the realities of unjust immunisation systems that can undermine trust and fuel vaccine hesitancy. A dedicated segment will address misinformation in faith communities, offering concrete examples and tools for constructive dialogue between faith and science. Through short inputs, panel discussions, and interactive dialogue, participants will identify practical, collaborative actions to strengthen and regain trust in public health and science, promote life‑saving vaccination, and ensure that immunisation systems are truly people‑centred and just. It is a call to reposition science as a gift from God, for sharing and furthering human dignity and wellbeing.
partners: World Council of Churches, World Health Organization
